title: Lesson 6: Scales
intro: Scales are the raw material of melodies and solos (see Scales and Keys (#/arts/music-theory/scales-and-keys)). On the guitar a scale is a fingering pattern in one hand position that moves to any key. Start with the minor pentatonic box, the most used scale shape in rock and blues, then the major scale.

items: Play the A minor pentatonic box and move it to other keys.
Play the G major scale in one position.
Hear how the same notes become a different mode over a different root.
Lesson 3 (note names), alternate picking from Lesson 2, and a metronome.
Step 1. Put finger 1 at fret 5 on string 6 (A, the root). The box covers frets 5 to 8: finger 1 plays fret 5, finger 3 fret 7, finger 4 fret 8.
Step 2. Play string 6 frets 5 and 8; string 5 frets 5 and 7; string 4 frets 5 and 7; string 3 frets 5 and 7; string 2 frets 5 and 8; string 1 frets 5 and 8. Two notes per string.
Step 3. Play it up and down with alternate picking, slowly, using Step ▶ to check each note. The roots (A) are on string 6 fret 5, string 4 fret 7 and string 1 fret 5: emphasise them.
Step 4. Add the 'blue note' (E♭, fret 6 on string 5) between frets 5 and 7 for the blues scale.
Step 5. Move the whole box so finger 1 is on another note of string 6: at fret 3 it is G minor pentatonic, at fret 8 C minor pentatonic.

examples.label: A blues lick with the blue note

blocks.alt: The neck from the nut to fret 17 with every note of A minor pentatonic as a labelled dot, the A's in red, and brackets marking boxes 1 to 5.
blocks.caption: The whole neck of A minor pentatonic in five boxes. When box 1 is comfortable, learn box 2 (frets 7–10), which overlaps it.

blocks.text: The major scale in one position

items: Step 1. G major, second position: finger 2 on string 6 fret 3 (G, the root). The pattern covers frets 2 to 5.
Step 2. String 6: frets 2, 3, 5 (F♯ G A). String 5: 2, 3, 5 (B C D). String 4: 2, 4, 5 (E F♯ G). String 3: 2, 4, 5 (A B C). String 2: 3, 5 (D E). String 1: 2, 3, 5 (F♯ G A).
Step 3. Play from the root G on string 6 up to G on string 1 (fret 3), saying 'do re mi fa sol la ti do' twice. Use Step ▶ to check.
Step 4. Move the pattern up two frets: A major. Up five frets from G: C major.

widget.title: G major, second position, two octaves

items: Step 1. Play the G major pattern again, but treat A as home: start and end on A (string 6 fret 5) and let the open A string ring underneath. The same notes now sound like A Dorian, minor with a bright sixth (see The Modes (#/arts/music-theory/scales-and-keys/modes)).
Step 2. Treat D as home (string 5 fret 5, open D string ringing): D Mixolydian, major with a flat seventh, the sound of a lot of rock.
Step 3. The fingering never changed; only the home note did. That is what a mode is.
3 min: A minor pentatonic box up and down, metronome 60, alternate picking.
3 min: the box at frets 3 (G) and 8 (C).
4 min: G major in second position, then A major two frets up.
3 min: improvise freely in the pentatonic box over a held open A string.

blocks.title: Move the box
blocks.text: Where is box 1 of E minor pentatonic, and of C minor pentatonic?
solution: Box 1 starts on the root on string 6. E: open string 6 (or fret 12), so the open position or frets 12–15. C: string 6 fret 8, so frets 8–11.

blocks.title: Relative
blocks.text: Which major pentatonic has exactly the same notes as A minor pentatonic?
solution: C major pentatonic (C D E G A), the relative major; in box 1 its roots are on string 6 fret 8, string 3 fret 5 and string 1 fret 8.

blocks.text: Sources: Goodrick, M. (1987). The Advancing Guitarist. Hal Leonard; Leavitt, W. G. (1966–1971). A Modern Method for Guitar, vols. 1–3. Berklee Press; Tagliarino, B. (2006). Guitar Fretboard Workbook. Hal Leonard; Levine, M. (1995). The Jazz Theory Book. Sher Music.
